newsitem.title: USA: EMU doubts cut both ways on German mark--U.S. pros.
newsitem.headline: EMU doubts cut both ways on German mark--U.S. pros.

text.p: A sudden wave of market pessimism over Europe's plans to unite under a common currency has both bloodied and bolstered the German mark, analysts said.

German economic woes have jeopardized the entire campaign toward European economic and monetary union (EMU) and triggered sharp selling of marks against the dollar, yen and British pound. As a result, a recent investor exodus from the lira and other peripheral European currencies to the mark has had only limited impact in bolstering the German unit overall.
Investors may still view Germany's mark as a safe haven from weakness elsewhere in Europe, but market players have found it increasingly necessary to seek refuge from Germany itself.

"We've seen some back-and-forth. Last week the lira and peseta were weak against the mark, but it had to come back a bit because the mark is so weak against the dollar," said Earl Johnson, foreign exchange economist at Bank of Montreal in Chicago.

Under a shower of EMU-dubious statements from officials in Germany and Italy last week, the mark/lira cross rate vaulted past 1,000 for the first time in three months and the mark surged against the Spanish peseta as well.
Dealers said this forced the central banks of Italy and Spain to defend their currencies in the open market.
That move clearly demonstrated the mark's residual value as continental Europe's backstop currency.
But the mark has also fallen to multi-year lows versus the dollar and sterling and an eight-month low against the yen.
Germany's record unemployment and meager growth prospects heighten the allure of steady-growth economies in the United States and Britain and even the beleaguered Japanese economy.

"There is a dollar/mark story, with (U.S.-German) bond spreads widening out, and the lower level in mark/yen suggests investors are even looking for yen under these circumstances," said Craig Larimer, head of international market analysis at First Chicago Capital Markets.

Much of continental Europe remains in a deep economic hole, severely reducing the chances that enough countries will meet EMU debt and deficit targets to make the single currency viable at its launch date of January 1999.
And while many analysts expect policy makers to bend the rules to allow Germany and France to participate, few see Italy and Spain granted such deference.

"The market has traded back and forth on whether the satellite countries can get in. But there's no way they're getting in by the start date," said Andrew Hodge, financial strategist at Bank Brussels Lambert in New York.

Many ordinary Germans as well as policy-makers have objected to calls for lowering the EMU entry bar, which would link Germany, and its traditionally strong currency, with less fiscally responsible nations.
In fact, each hint of German resistance to a back-door Italian EMU entry, or watering down of the criteria in general, clearly boosts the mark's prospects, Hodge said.

"When we see news of EMU not happening, it would typically tend to strengthen Germany, and we definitely have seen a rise in pessimism that this commom currency is going to get done on time," he added.
In addition to weakening Germany's economic hand, EMU would also eliminate the need for other European nations to hold marks in reserve.

And while officials were publicly casting doubts on EMU's fate, reports had some European central banks quietly selling marks last week to switch reserves to the dollar and other units, analysts said.
Those sales may explain part of the mark's recent torpor.
"There had been signs that some countries were changing their reserve mix by selling marks and buying dollars and other currencies," Hodge said. "We heard of a fair amount of selling on that score."
